title: Short Stuff: In-Flight Entertainment
summary: Short Stuff episode with Josh and Chuck (Jerry sitting in for Dave) on in-flight entertainment. They cover the history of airline movies from the one-movie-for-the-whole-plane era (first in-flight movie in 1929, real movie service from the early 1960s) to today's seatback streaming, licensing and equipment costs, the weight-savings argument from a Norwegian economist, "airplane movies," airline edited versions and cultural sensitivities by region, Delta's edit of the film Carol, the 2007 Family Friendly Flies Act, and a study comparing movie running times on Virgin Atlantic and Air Canada.

segments.title: Opening and memories of old in-flight movies
segments.summary: Josh introduces the short on in-flight movies. Chuck recalls the old days of one movie shown on big overhead screens, and Josh describes shared headphones and the single movie everyone watched.

segments.title: History and modern in-flight entertainment
segments.summary: Chuck says the first in-flight movie was in 1929, a newsreel and cartoons on a transcontinental air transport flight, and that real movie service began in the early 1960s. He describes modern systems with broadband, onboard servers, streaming movies, games, ebooks and podcasts.

segments.title: Costs of in-flight movie systems
segments.summary: The hosts discuss licensing costs, roughly twenty million dollars a year for content for some airlines, and equipment costs of about five million dollars per aircraft. A Norwegian economics professor calculated that removing the system could save about three million dollars per year per aircraft in weight and cost. Licensing models include flat fees and per-view charges.

segments.title: Airplane movies
segments.summary: Chuck describes airplane movies as films you would not pay to see in a theater but will watch on a flight. He mentions watching the film F1 on a recent flight.

segments.title: Viewing F1 on a plane
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck discuss the F1 movie. Josh says it had too much minimalist office stuff, and Chuck says the racing was great but the explanations of Formula One rules were excessive.

segments.title: Break and transition to airline edits
segments.summary: The hosts take a short break and tease the segment on how airlines avoid offending passengers with movie content.

segments.title: Airline edited movies and regional sensitivities
segments.summary: Josh explains airline versions of movies, made by editing companies or studios, which remove sexual, violent, gory or offensive content. Chuck covers regional differences: Europe is more tolerant of nudity but less of gore, the Middle East avoids bare skin and sexy content but tolerates violence more, and airlines serving many Muslim passengers edit out references to pork. Josh notes Singapore is sensitive to LGBTQ content, though the hosts say that is not the case, and that language edits are less common now that movies are streamed to headphones.

segments.title: Passenger warnings, Delta and Carol, and the Airline Passenger Experience Association
segments.summary: Chuck describes content warnings shown before movies and the Airline Passenger Experience Association, which offers guidance to distributors and airlines. He cites Delta facing criticism in 2015 for editing kissing scenes from the film Carol. Josh says a Global Eagle executive said airlines have a lot of say in edits, with Delta more conservative and American and United more permissive.

segments.title: Family Friendly Flies Act
segments.summary: Chuck describes a 2007 co-sponsored bill, the Family Friendly Flies Act, that would have created child-safe viewing areas with no content above G rating, which did not pass. Josh notes it came from North Carolina congressmen and that the compromise idea was PG-13 movies.

segments.title: Movie running times on Virgin and Air Canada
segments.summary: Chuck reports a study comparing running times on Virgin and Air Canada: two thirds of movies matched theatrical length, 14 percent were shorter due to edits, and 21 percent were longer. Josh comments that Virgin is probably not heavy on editing and the hosts plan a Canadian tour.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Chuck closes the short and gives the iHeartRadio credit line.
